title: Navigation for an architecture studio
metaTitle: Navigation for an architecture studio site
excerpt: Navigation should map the jobs a client has: see the work, understand the offer, and start a project. Labels need to match words they already use.
alt: A wide mountain valley with snowy peaks, a braided river, and evergreen trees in the foreground, a landscape that only helps if someone can tell which path to take.
caption: A valley with more than one way through. The menu should still be obvious. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What labels belong in the menu?
faqs.answer: Use the jobs a client already has words for: Work, the practice, and Start a project as a persistent action. Journal, awards, and a manifesto can wait off that primary list until the work is easy to find. If a label needs a translation, it is not ready for the header.

faqs.question: How many items is too many?
faqs.answer: If a client cannot see the work and the way to start a conversation without opening a second panel, the menu is doing too much. Five clear items beat twelve clever ones. On a phone, the cost of an extra item is higher because the list covers the projects.

faqs.question: Should project types be in the header?
faqs.answer: Put them in the header when you want to be hired for those types and a client would look for them by name. Houses, alterations, interiors. Keep a single Work item when the archive is small and the types would be three lonely pages. The test is the word the client would type or say.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
The architecture studio website navigation should be a map of jobs, not a list of departments. A client judging taste before competence already has the words. Work. Houses, or whatever you actually take. A way to start a project conversation. The labels should match those words. One path should begin the conversation without a hunt.

A poetic menu reassures the office that the site has a voice. It slows the client who came to see if you can handle their site. They should not have to decode you before they can judge you.

## Jobs, not departments

List the reasons a careful client opens the site. They want to see built work. They want to know what kinds of commissions you take. They want to know a person stands behind it. They want to start a conversation if the fit is real. Those are the items. "Philosophy," "Insights," "Culture," and "Explore" are departments the office invented.

A practical primary list:

- Work
- The offers you want, if they are not obvious inside Work
- The practice, under a human label such as Practice or People
- Start a project

Four is plenty. Add Journal only when you publish on a rhythm you will keep, and only if those essays help a client decide. A dead journal in the header is a promise of thought you are not keeping.

[The W3C's WCAG overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) groups requirements under four principles: perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. Navigation sits in all four, and understandable is the one studios skip. A control should say where it goes. A person using a keyboard should be able to reach it. The same items should show up in the same places, so the site is predictable. Clever labels fail the understandable test first.

[Google's guidance on title links](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) asks for descriptive, concise titles. The same standard belongs on menu items. "Work" is concise and true. "Selected spatial essays" is a title that makes the reader guess. If the page heading and the menu item disagree, fix the menu. The client remembers the item they clicked.

## Words they already use

Listen to the first emails you receive. People say extension, renovation, new build, fit-out, granny flat, apartment. Use the word your clients use in your city. A practice in one country should not import another's professional jargon into the menu to sound stricter.

If you have three real lines of work, they can be children of Work, visible on hover or as a simple list on the work index. Do not hide them behind a single image map. A client looking for alterations should see the word Alterations as text.

Match the menu to the services page. If the services page says "Alterations" and the menu says "Transform," you have split the practice in two. Pick the plainer word and use it in the menu, the heading, and the button.

Proper names of projects belong in the work index, not in the global menu, unless you have so few that the menu is the index. Five houses can be the menu. Fifty cannot. The global menu is for types and actions. The index is for titles.

Test the labels on someone who has not seen the design. Ask them to find a house alteration and to start a project. If they hesitate, the label is performing. Change the word, not the client's patience.

## One path that starts a project

One item is an action, and it should look like an action. Start a project. It can sit at the end of the list, in a persistent corner, or both, as long as the words match. "Contact," "Inquire," "Connect," and "Hello" are four different temperatures. Choose the one that means a real job, and delete the others.

Do not make the action a treasure hunt at the footer only. A client who has decided halfway down a project page will not always finish the essay. The path should survive on the project page, the work index, and the practice page.

The destination is a short conversation starter, not a new miniature site. Say what to send. Do not ask them to pick a department from a dropdown of twelve services you barely offer. If the offers are houses and alterations, those two choices are enough.

On a phone, the action should be visible without opening the full menu if you can do it cleanly. A bar with Work and Start a project, plus a menu for the rest, is often enough. A hamburger that hides everything, including the work, punishes the client who is judging you in a taxi.

If the menu and the page have drifted, and you want to settle the labels before a redesign, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the current header and the last ten client emails. The call should end with the words you will actually use, and with a sense of whether the site is a relabel or a rebuild. Hanabi designs and builds. The menu is a writing decision before it is a component.

## Work first

The first item should be the work, for this buyer. They came for taste, and they will judge competence from how the work is framed. A menu that leads with Journal, Shop, or a film forces them to be fans before they are clients. Some practices want fans. The client with a site still needs the projects in one click.

Inside Work, sort in a way a client can use. By type, then by year. Or by a short set of constraints: tight sites, alterations, interiors. Do not sort only by the date you photographed them, if that hides the only alteration under a run of new houses. The sort is an argument about what you want next.

Selected projects on the homepage are not a substitute for a clear Work item. The homepage is a sample. The menu promises the rest. If Work leads to a page with three images and no names, the menu has over-promised. Fix the page or rename the item.

Search within the site is optional at this scale. A good index beats a search box that cannot spell a project name. Add search when the archive is too long to scan. Do not add it to look complete.

## The menu on a phone

Design the small screen as the real menu, not as a collapsed desktop. List the items in the same order. Keep type large enough to tap without hitting two links. Leave the project photographs alone until the menu is closed. A menu that is a translucent layer over a moving film is a way to miss.

The open state should trap focus for keyboard users and be dismissible. Those are ordinary quality bars, and they matter on a site a client may tab through on a laptop as well. WCAG's operable principle is the reminder: people have to be able to use the control, not only see it.

Do not put a different information architecture on the phone. A desktop with seven items and a phone with three, hiding People and the fee, trains the office to ignore half its clients. If an item does not deserve a place on the phone, it does not deserve a place in the header.

Check the menu with one thumb, outdoors, on a bright day. If you cannot find Start a project in a few seconds, a client comparing three offices will not try harder. They will go to the next site. The valley can have many paths. The menu should not.

## Labels that fail this client

A few patterns show up often, and they fail the same way. They ask the client to admire the practice before they can use it.

"Explore" as the path to projects. Explore what? The word withholds the job.

A single item called Studio that contains people, fees, jobs, and the journal. That is a drawer, not a label.

Icon-only navigation. A house icon is not a label for a house practice. Text is the label. An icon can sit beside it if it helps, and it still needs an accessible name.

A menu that changes per page to be contextual, with no stable way home to the work. Contextual links inside a project are good. A shifting global menu is how people get lost.

Dropdowns that open on hover and close before a click. They fail on touch and they fail anyone moving quickly. Click or tap to open, and keep the list still.

If the office loves a poetic word, let it live in a sentence on the practice page. The menu is infrastructure. Infrastructure should be dull and exact.

## The pictures those labels open

A clear menu still delivers the reader to images. If Work opens on a fullscreen render with no project name, the navigation did its job and the photography undid it. The next decision is what the pictures argue, and which frames you refuse.

That is [photography direction for an architecture studio](/blog/photography-direction-for-an-architecture-studio). Set the labels first so the pictures have a place to land. Then make sure the landing is a building with a constraint, not a mood with a menu.
